doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Founding the Jazz Journalists Association and championing musicians like Rubalcaba
summary: He tells of the JJA's origin, networking aims, and his support for Gonzalo Rubalcaba, Andrew Hill, Sonny Criss and Grover Washington.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: of our vast experience. The networking aspect, the Jazz Journalists Association started in ’85 at a meeting in Chicago that brought together writers and broadcasters. I think it was sponsored by the NEA. And we decided that we should have some sort of organization, mostly just for networking purposes. So if we go to a city that we’re not familiar with for a festival we’ve got somebody to go out to dinner with. And it’s worked very well that way. And of course I think that jazz journalists have often been people who did not engage successfully in social functions as teenagers. You know, instead they sat in their rooms listening to their records. And I think that giving them a safe social forum is a good thing and suggest to them that this is not a sin that they’re sitting listening to their records but that a lot of us do it and it’s sort of a normal behavior and it’s got a valuable place in our society. They don’t have to hide it or be ashamed of it, and that they could actually ask for decent money or working conditions, you know, if they’re going to pursue this that they are professionals, that they can meet some professional standards and we can talk about what kind of professional standards we’d like to see imposed on our profession, like to be established. So it’s worked in a lot of those ways. And also informs the general public and the musician about what it is we do. We do that through out web site, we expose a lot of new music. It’s the journalists who discover the talent and bring it to the attention of the record companies often, the booking agents, the concert producers. If I get enthusiastic about a young band I let people know about it. Gonzalo Rubalcaba, who I’ve written about quite a lot, I heard him in ’85 in Berlin when he was doing his electric Cuban sort of fusion thing. And I didn’t think so much of it at that time. Then I guess I heard about him through Charlie Haden, mentioned him to me, and I saw him do a recording here in Toronto when he couldn’t come into the US. I was invited to go to the studio and hear him with DeJohnette and Charlie Haden and I thought it was great. “The Blessing” is the album that came out of that. And I started writing about him and I think he’s just a wonderful pianist and I’ve followed his career and I think he’s a substantial performer. I’ve written about him a couple of times for Down Beat and I’ve written about him for other publications, and I guess I’ve written his liner notes also. And after a while it accrues some substance to support this person. If Howard Mandel likes him in this way, well maybe there’s something there we should pay some attention to. Don Pullen. Andrew Hill. Andrew is very grateful to me and I’m proud of that. Andrew says you stopped writing about me — “All the articles until you wrote about me, Howard, were about me as a performer in the sixties. You brought me up to date.” And I don’t know I think I’ve been very lucky to run into some musicians I could do that with. Sonny Criss, I wrote about for Down Beat early on.
